presentation: Testing for coeliac disease on a gluten-containing diet
stem:
A 26-year-old man asks his GP for a diagnosis after months of loose stools, wind and bloating. On a friend's advice he stopped eating bread and pasta a few weeks ago and feels much better. Examination is normal.

Which condition should be tested for, with the advice that he must eat gluten again in the weeks before the test?
why_correct: Symptoms that settle when wheat is removed raise the possibility of coeliac disease, which must be confirmed or excluded properly because it needs lifelong strict treatment and follow-up. Serology and duodenal biopsy become falsely negative once gluten is withdrawn, so he must reintroduce gluten before testing. Self-diagnosis on a gluten-free diet risks a missed or wrong diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Lactose intolerance is related to dairy, not wheat, and is not tested with a gluten challenge. C. Irritable bowel syndrome is diagnosed clinically and coeliac disease must be excluded first. D. Chronic pancreatitis causes steatorrhoea and pain, usually with heavy alcohol use, and is not linked to wheat. E. Microscopic colitis causes watery diarrhoea, usually in older adults, and does not depend on gluten.
pearl: NICE advises eating gluten in more than one meal every day for at least 6 weeks before coeliac serology.
thinking: Chronic bloating and loose stools ↓ Improvement after cutting out wheat ↓ Suggests coeliac disease ↓ Tests become falsely negative without gluten ↓ Reintroduce gluten, then test
exam_trap: C, Irritable bowel syndrome — many people with IBS feel better after cutting wheat, but coeliac disease must be excluded before an IBS label is given.
takeaway: Test for coeliac disease only while the patient is eating gluten, as a gluten-free diet makes the tests unreliable.

stem:
A 38-year-old woman calls NHS 111 late in the evening with severe, constant pain under her right ribs that began an hour after a fish and chip supper. She has had similar attacks over the last few months, each lasting a few hours and settling on their own. She has no fever and has not noticed yellowing of her eyes.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
correct_answer: E. Biliary colic due to gallstones
why_correct: Biliary colic is caused by a gallstone transiently blocking the cystic duct, often triggered by a fatty meal that stimulates gallbladder contraction. The pain is constant despite its name, felt in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium, and lasts minutes to a few hours before resolving. Recurrent self-limiting episodes without fever or jaundice fit uncomplicated gallstone disease.
why_wrong: A. Peptic ulcer pain is epigastric and burning, often linked to hunger or relieved by food or antacids, rather than discrete attacks lasting hours. B. Ureteric colic is loin-to-groin pain and is not triggered by meals. C. Irritable bowel syndrome causes lower abdominal pain related to defecation. D. Appendicitis is a single progressive illness with right iliac fossa pain, not recurrent self-limiting attacks.
pearl: Ultrasound of the abdomen is the first-line imaging for suspected gallstones, and laparoscopic cholecystectomy is offered for symptomatic gallstones.
thinking: Right upper quadrant pain after a fatty meal ↓ Constant pain lasting a few hours ↓ Recurrent attacks that settle ↓ No fever or jaundice ↓ Uncomplicated biliary colic from gallstones
exam_trap: A, Peptic ulcer disease — upper abdominal pain linked to food is tempting, but the right upper quadrant site, fatty meal trigger and discrete attacks lasting hours point to the gallbladder.
takeaway: Recurrent constant right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals, settling within hours, suggests biliary colic.

stem:
A 34-year-old man calls NHS 111 for advice. For several months he has had wind, loose stools and tiredness, and a friend with coeliac disease has suggested he cut out bread, pasta and beer straight away. His GP has already arranged blood tests for next week to look for coeliac disease.

What advice should he be given about his diet in the meantime?

options.A: Cut out wheat, barley and rye now so the blood test is easier to interpret
options.B: Switch to a low-FODMAP diet until the results are back
options.C: Stop all milk and cheese as well as gluten before the blood test
options.D: Eat only rice and potatoes for the week before the appointment
options.E: Keep eating foods that contain gluten until all coeliac testing is finished

correct_answer: E. Keep eating foods that contain gluten until all coeliac testing is finished
why_correct: Coeliac serology and duodenal biopsy both depend on an ongoing immune response to gluten. If he removes gluten before testing, antibody levels fall and the villi start to heal, so a false-negative result becomes likely. NICE advises eating gluten in more than one meal every day for at least six weeks before testing.
why_wrong: A. Removing gluten before testing makes a false-negative result more likely, not easier to interpret. B. A low-FODMAP diet cuts many wheat products and may blunt the antibody response; it is not a step to take before coeliac testing. C. Dairy exclusion has no role in coeliac testing and only adds unnecessary restriction. D. A rice and potato diet is effectively gluten-free and would undermine the test.
pearl: If someone has already gone gluten-free and is reluctant to restart gluten, refer to gastroenterology rather than testing them on a gluten-free diet.
thinking: Suspected coeliac disease with tests booked ↓ Serology and biopsy rely on an active immune response to gluten ↓ Excluding gluten lowers antibodies and lets the mucosa recover ↓ This produces false-negative results ↓ Advise continuing gluten in more than one meal a day until testing is complete
exam_trap: A, Cutting out wheat, barley and rye now — it feels sensible because gluten is the likely trigger, but doing it before the tests can mask the disease and delay a firm diagnosis.
takeaway: Keep eating gluten until coeliac serology and any biopsy have been completed.

stem:
A 19-year-old man with newly confirmed coeliac disease is seen by the practice dietitian. He wants to know exactly what he must avoid, because he has noticed that toast, beer and breakfast cereals made from barley all leave him bloated with loose stools.

Which dietary component drives the immune reaction in his condition?
why_correct: Coeliac disease is an autoimmune enteropathy triggered by gluten, a group of proteins found in wheat, barley and rye. Gliadin peptides are deamidated by tissue transglutaminase and presented to T cells, causing villous atrophy in the small intestine. His symptoms after wheat toast, beer and barley cereal fit this exactly.
why_wrong: A. Lactose is a sugar; lactose intolerance can coexist with coeliac disease but does not cause it. C. Casein is a milk protein relevant to cow's milk protein allergy, not coeliac disease. D. Fructose malabsorption can cause bloating but is not an immune trigger and would not explain reactions to beer and barley. E. Ovalbumin is an egg protein linked to egg allergy.
pearl: Pure oats are tolerated by most people with coeliac disease, but contamination with wheat is common, so only oats labelled gluten-free should be used.
thinking: Symptoms after wheat, barley and beer ↓ Common element is gluten-containing cereals ↓ Coeliac disease is an immune response to gluten (gliadin) ↓ Tissue transglutaminase is the autoantigen ↓ Gluten is the trigger
exam_trap: A, Lactose — bloating and loose stools also suggest lactose intolerance, and secondary lactase deficiency often accompanies untreated coeliac disease, but lactose is not the antigen that drives it.
takeaway: Coeliac disease is an immune-mediated reaction to gluten in wheat, barley and rye.
notes: Reviewer fix: Stem asked for a 'dietary protein' while lactose/fructose distractors are sugars; changed to 'dietary component' so options are homogeneous

presentation: Excluding coeliac disease before diagnosing IBS
stem:
A 46-year-old man attends a follow-up GP appointment. For a year he has had episodes of crampy abdominal pain relieved by opening his bowels, with bloating and loose stools, and he has found they ease when he avoids bread and pasta. He has not lost weight, has no blood in his stools and his blood count is normal. The GP is considering a diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome.

Which condition should be tested for before this label is applied?
why_correct: NICE advises that coeliac serology should be offered to anyone with symptoms suggestive of irritable bowel syndrome before the diagnosis is made. Coeliac disease commonly mimics IBS with bloating, pain and altered bowel habit, and improvement on avoiding wheat makes it more relevant here. Missing it leaves a treatable autoimmune condition, with risks of anaemia and osteoporosis, undiagnosed.
why_wrong: A. Lactose intolerance can cause similar symptoms but is linked to dairy rather than bread and pasta, and is not part of the routine tests before diagnosing IBS. C. Pancreatic insufficiency causes steatorrhoea and weight loss and is not a routine exclusion in a well man. D. Diverticular disease would not explain improvement on avoiding wheat and is not routinely tested for. E. Bile acid malabsorption is considered for refractory diarrhoea rather than as a routine first exclusion.
pearl: Before diagnosing IBS, NICE recommends a full blood count, ESR or CRP and coeliac serology, plus faecal calprotectin when inflammatory bowel disease is a possibility in younger adults.
thinking: Chronic pain, bloating and loose stools without red flags ↓ IBS looks likely ↓ Improvement off wheat raises coeliac disease ↓ Coeliac disease commonly mimics IBS ↓ Check coeliac serology while still eating gluten before diagnosing IBS
exam_trap: A, Lactose intolerance — food-related bloating suggests it, but the link here is to wheat products, and coeliac serology is the test specifically recommended before an IBS diagnosis.
takeaway: Always test for coeliac disease before labelling someone as having irritable bowel syndrome.

stem:
A 26-year-old man is seen in the gastroenterology rapid-access clinic. Over two months he has been passing loose stools mixed with fresh blood several times a day, often has to rush to the toilet, and feels he has not finished after each visit. Stool cultures are negative and he has not travelled.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Chronic bloody diarrhoea with urgency and tenesmus in a young adult, with negative stool cultures, points to inflammation that starts in the rectum and extends proximally, which is typical of ulcerative colitis. The rectal involvement explains the urgency and the feeling of incomplete emptying. He needs faecal calprotectin, bloods and colonoscopy with biopsies to confirm it.
why_wrong: B. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause rectal bleeding, and blood in the stool should prompt investigation for another cause. C. Haemorrhoids cause bright red blood on the paper or in the pan but not persistent bloody diarrhoea with urgency. D. Coeliac disease causes malabsorption and loose stools but not visible blood. E. Diverticulitis is unusual at this age and presents with left iliac fossa pain and fever rather than months of bloody diarrhoea.
pearl: Smoking appears to protect against ulcerative colitis, whereas it worsens Crohn's disease; some people first develop colitis after stopping smoking.
thinking: Young adult with months of bloody diarrhoea ↓ Urgency and tenesmus suggest rectal inflammation ↓ Negative cultures and no travel make infection unlikely ↓ Continuous colitis starting at the rectum ↓ Ulcerative colitis
exam_trap: C, Haemorrhoidal disease — rectal bleeding in a young person is often from haemorrhoids, but they do not cause chronic diarrhoea, urgency and tenesmus.
takeaway: Chronic bloody diarrhoea with urgency and tenesmus in a young adult suggests ulcerative colitis.

stem:
A 37-year-old man with known left-sided colitis attends the emergency department. Over three days his bowels have opened about ten times a day with blood in every stool. He feels hot and shaky, his heart rate is fast, and his lower abdomen is tender on palpation but not distended. His CRP is markedly raised.

Which complication has he most likely developed?

options.A: Infective gastroenteritis unrelated to his colitis

why_correct: Frequent bloody stools together with signs of systemic toxicity such as fever, tachycardia and raised inflammatory markers meet the Truelove and Witts criteria for acute severe ulcerative colitis. This is a medical emergency that needs admission, intravenous corticosteroids, stool tests to exclude infection, thromboprophylaxis and joint medical and surgical care. The absence of distension makes toxic megacolon less likely, but it must be checked for with an abdominal X-ray.
why_wrong: A. Infection, including Clostridioides difficile, must be excluded with stool tests, but a flare of known colitis with systemic upset is the main concern. B. IBS does not cause bloody diarrhoea, fever or raised CRP. C. Colorectal cancer does not cause an abrupt illness with fever and ten bloody stools a day. E. Ischaemic colitis occurs mainly in older people with vascular disease and presents with sudden pain and bleeding rather than a flare of known colitis.
pearl: If there is no adequate response to intravenous steroids after about three days, rescue therapy with ciclosporin or infliximab, or colectomy, should be considered.
thinking: Known ulcerative colitis ↓ Six or more bloody stools a day ↓ Fever, tachycardia and raised CRP indicate systemic toxicity ↓ Meets criteria for a severe flare ↓ Acute severe ulcerative colitis needing admission and IV steroids
exam_trap: A, Infective gastroenteritis — infection must always be excluded in a flare, but labelling this as a separate infection risks delaying steroids for a life-threatening colitis flare.
takeaway: Frequent bloody stools with fever, tachycardia or raised CRP in ulcerative colitis means acute severe colitis and needs admission.

stem:
A 58-year-old man with radiation proctitis after treatment for prostate cancer tells the nurse specialist that he keeps straining on the toilet because it feels as though there is still stool to pass, even though very little comes out.

What is the term for this symptom?
why_correct: Tenesmus is a persistent or recurrent sensation of incomplete rectal emptying, often with straining, when little or no stool is present. It reflects irritation or inflammation of the rectum, as in proctitis from radiotherapy, ulcerative colitis or infection, and can also occur with a rectal tumour.
why_wrong: A. Urgency is a sudden need to reach the toilet, not a feeling of incomplete emptying afterwards. B. Dyschezia means painful or difficult defecation. C. Steatorrhoea describes pale, greasy, foul-smelling stools from fat malabsorption. E. Obstipation is severe constipation with failure to pass stool or wind.
pearl: New tenesmus in an older adult without a known cause should prompt examination and investigation for a low rectal cancer.
thinking: Rectal inflammation after radiotherapy ↓ Feeling of unfinished evacuation ↓ Straining with little stool produced ↓ Defined as tenesmus
exam_trap: A, Faecal urgency — urgency and tenesmus often occur together in proctitis, but urgency is the sudden need to go, not the feeling of incomplete emptying.
takeaway: Tenesmus is the sensation of incomplete rectal emptying despite little or no stool being present.

stem:
A 33-year-old woman with a flare of proctosigmoiditis tells her IBD nurse that whenever she feels the need to open her bowels she has only seconds to get to a toilet, and she now plans every journey around where toilets are. She has not actually soiled herself.

Which term best describes this symptom?
why_correct: Faecal urgency is a sudden, compelling need to defecate that is difficult to defer. It is caused by an inflamed, poorly compliant rectum, which is why it is a key marker of activity in ulcerative colitis and proctitis. She has not lost control of stool, so incontinence is not the right term.
why_wrong: B. Incontinence means involuntary loss of stool, which she has not had. C. Tenesmus is the feeling of incomplete emptying after defecation, not the rush to get there. D. Dyschezia is pain or difficulty with defecation. E. Faecal loading describes retained stool in constipation.
pearl: Urgency is one of the symptoms that most affects quality of life in ulcerative colitis and is increasingly used as an outcome in assessing disease activity.
thinking: Active rectal and sigmoid inflammation ↓ Sudden compelling urge to defecate ↓ Hard to delay but no soiling ↓ Defined as faecal urgency
exam_trap: B, Faecal incontinence — urgency can progress to incontinence, but she has not lost control of stool, so the term does not apply.
takeaway: Faecal urgency is a sudden need to defecate that is hard to delay, typical of rectal inflammation.

stem:
A 36-year-old man has had a confirmed diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome for eight years, with normal blood tests, coeliac serology and faecal calprotectin. His uncle has just been diagnosed with bowel cancer and he asks the practice nurse whether his long-standing IBS means he is more likely to develop it too.

What is the most accurate reply?

options.A: IBS raises the risk once symptoms have lasted more than five years
options.B: IBS is a precursor of colonic polyps
options.C: IBS requires colonoscopic surveillance every three years
options.D: IBS roughly doubles lifetime bowel cancer risk
options.E: IBS is not linked to an increased risk of bowel cancer

correct_answer: E. IBS is not linked to an increased risk of bowel cancer
why_correct: Irritable bowel syndrome is a disorder of gut-brain interaction without structural or inflammatory damage to the bowel, so it does not increase colorectal cancer risk however long it lasts. His own risk depends on factors such as age and family history, which can be discussed separately. He should still be told to seek review if new red flag features develop, such as rectal bleeding or weight loss.
why_wrong: A. Duration of IBS symptoms does not confer cancer risk. B. IBS does not cause polyps. C. IBS has no surveillance programme; surveillance is for conditions such as long-standing colitis or previous adenomas. D. There is no evidence that IBS increases lifetime colorectal cancer risk.
pearl: Long-standing extensive ulcerative colitis or Crohn's colitis does increase colorectal cancer risk, which is why it is important not to confuse IBS with inflammatory bowel disease.
thinking: Established IBS with normal investigations ↓ Functional disorder without mucosal damage ↓ No increased colorectal cancer risk ↓ Advise on red flags and discuss family history separately
exam_trap: D, IBS roughly doubles lifetime risk — chronic bowel symptoms seem as though they should carry risk, as they do in inflammatory bowel disease, but IBS has no such link.
takeaway: Irritable bowel syndrome does not increase the risk of colorectal cancer.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman who rarely drinks alcohol is admitted from the emergency department with severe epigastric pain going through to her back and vomiting. Her serum amylase is markedly raised. She has had several episodes of right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals over the past year.

Which underlying cause of her pancreatitis is most likely?
why_correct: Gallstones are the most common cause of acute pancreatitis in the UK, alongside alcohol. A woman with little alcohol intake and previous episodes typical of biliary colic most likely has a stone that has passed into the common bile duct and obstructed pancreatic drainage. She needs an abdominal ultrasound and, once recovered, cholecystectomy during the same admission or soon after to prevent recurrence.
why_wrong: A. Hypercalcaemia is a recognised but uncommon cause, and nothing here suggests it. C. Very high triglycerides can cause pancreatitis but are much less common than gallstones and there are no clues pointing to them. D. Mumps is a rare cause, mostly in children and young adults. E. Azathioprine can cause pancreatitis, but she is not taking it.
pearl: Patients with gallstone pancreatitis should have cholecystectomy during the index admission or within two weeks of discharge to reduce the risk of further attacks.
thinking: Epigastric pain radiating to the back with raised amylase ↓ Acute pancreatitis ↓ Minimal alcohol intake ↓ Previous post-prandial right upper quadrant pain suggests gallstones ↓ Gallstone pancreatitis
exam_trap: C, Hypertriglyceridaemia — it is a well-known cause, but it is much rarer than gallstones and her history of biliary pain points clearly to stones.
takeaway: Gallstones and alcohol are the commonest causes of acute pancreatitis in the UK.

presentation: FIT to guide suspected colorectal cancer referral
stem:
A 59-year-old woman attends her GP because her stools have been looser and more frequent for two months. She has noticed no blood. A full blood count arranged last week shows a low haemoglobin with low ferritin, and she is not menstruating.

What test should the GP request to help guide referral on the suspected cancer pathway?

options.B: CT colonography arranged directly from primary care

why_correct: NICE NG12 recommends a quantitative faecal immunochemical test (FIT) in primary care to guide referral for suspected colorectal cancer in adults with symptoms such as a change in bowel habit or iron-deficiency anaemia. The FIT result, alongside the clinical picture, helps decide whether she needs an urgent suspected cancer referral. Her unexplained iron deficiency also needs investigating in its own right.
why_wrong: A. Tumour markers such as CA 19-9 are not used to diagnose or triage suspected bowel cancer. B. Imaging is arranged by the secondary care pathway after referral, not as the primary care triage test. D. Guaiac faecal occult blood testing has been replaced by quantitative FIT because it is less accurate. E. Stool culture looks for infection and does not assess cancer risk.
pearl: A negative FIT does not completely exclude colorectal cancer; if clinical concern persists, safety-net and consider referral anyway.
thinking: New change in bowel habit ↓ Iron-deficiency anaemia in a postmenopausal woman ↓ Symptoms that may represent colorectal cancer ↓ NICE advises quantitative FIT to guide referral ↓ Request FIT and refer according to the result and clinical concern
exam_trap: B, CT colonography from primary care — imaging seems like a direct route to a diagnosis, but NICE uses FIT as the primary care test to prioritise referral, with imaging or colonoscopy arranged by the specialist pathway.
takeaway: Quantitative FIT is the primary care test that guides referral for suspected colorectal cancer.

stem:
A 63-year-old man has had generalised itching for several weeks and has noticed pale stools and dark urine. He is not jaundiced to look at yet. His GP orders liver function tests.

Which result pattern would best fit an obstructive (cholestatic) picture?

options.A: Very high ALT and AST with near-normal ALP
options.B: Isolated rise in unconjugated bilirubin with normal enzymes
options.C: Low albumin with a prolonged prothrombin time only
options.D: Disproportionate rise in ALP with a raised GGT
options.E: Raised AST greater than twice ALT with a normal ALP

correct_answer: D. Disproportionate rise in ALP with a raised GGT
why_correct: Cholestasis, whether from a blocked bile duct or intrahepatic disease, causes alkaline phosphatase to rise more than the transaminases. A raised GGT alongside it confirms that the ALP is from the liver rather than bone. Itching, pale stools and dark urine support impaired bile flow, so he needs an abdominal ultrasound to look for duct dilatation.
why_wrong: A. A predominant transaminase rise indicates hepatocellular injury, such as hepatitis. B. Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia suggests Gilbert syndrome or haemolysis, not cholestasis. C. Low albumin and prolonged clotting reflect impaired synthetic function rather than the pattern of injury. E. An AST to ALT ratio above two suggests alcohol-related liver disease.
pearl: In a painless obstructive picture with weight loss in an older adult, consider pancreatic head cancer and arrange urgent imaging.
thinking: Itch, pale stools and dark urine ↓ Suggests impaired bile flow ↓ Cholestasis raises ALP more than ALT ↓ GGT confirms a hepatic source of ALP ↓ Obstructive pattern; arrange ultrasound
exam_trap: A, Very high ALT and AST — liver disease brings transaminases to mind, but a transaminase-led rise indicates hepatocellular damage rather than cholestasis.
takeaway: A cholestatic picture is a predominant rise in ALP with a raised GGT.

presentation: Colorectal cancer risk in long-standing colitis
stem:
A 48-year-old man has had ulcerative colitis affecting his whole colon since he was 30. His symptoms are well controlled on mesalazine, and he asks his gastroenterologist why he has been invited for regular colonoscopies when he feels fine.

Which long-term risk is the surveillance designed to detect?
why_correct: Long-standing extensive ulcerative colitis increases the risk of colorectal dysplasia and cancer, and the risk rises with the duration and extent of disease and with poorly controlled inflammation. NICE and BSG recommend colonoscopic surveillance starting around ten years after symptom onset in people with colitis beyond the rectum. Surveillance aims to detect dysplasia early, when it can be removed or treated.
why_wrong: A. Small bowel lymphoma is linked to coeliac disease rather than colitis. B. Ischaemic colitis is related to vascular disease, not long-standing ulcerative colitis. C. Diverticular disease is common with age but is not a complication of colitis and is not a reason for surveillance. D. Anal fissure is a local, benign problem and does not need colonoscopic surveillance.
pearl: Coexisting primary sclerosing cholangitis greatly increases colorectal cancer risk in colitis, and these patients need annual colonoscopic surveillance from diagnosis.
thinking: Extensive colitis for nearly two decades ↓ Chronic inflammation drives dysplasia ↓ Increased colorectal cancer risk ↓ Surveillance colonoscopy detects dysplasia early
exam_trap: A, Small bowel lymphoma — inflammatory gut disease and lymphoma are linked in coeliac disease, but the key malignancy in long-standing colitis is colorectal cancer.
takeaway: Long-standing extensive ulcerative colitis increases colorectal cancer risk, so colonoscopic surveillance is offered.

stem:
A 22-year-old man who smokes sees his GP with five months of loose stools, cramping pain in the right lower abdomen after meals and a loss of nearly a stone in weight. He has had no blood in his stools. On examination there is fullness in the right iliac fossa.

Which diagnosis is most important to consider?
why_correct: Months of diarrhoea with right-sided abdominal pain, weight loss and a right iliac fossa mass in a young smoker suggest terminal ileal Crohn's disease. Smoking increases the risk and severity of Crohn's disease. He needs faecal calprotectin, blood tests and urgent referral to gastroenterology for ileocolonoscopy and small bowel imaging.
why_wrong: A. Weight loss and a palpable mass are red flags that do not fit irritable bowel syndrome. B. Appendicitis is an acute illness over hours to days, not five months of symptoms. C. Coeliac disease causes diarrhoea and weight loss but not a right iliac fossa mass. D. Ulcerative colitis usually presents with bloody diarrhoea and does not cause an ileal mass.
pearl: Unlike ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease is made worse by smoking, and stopping smoking is one of the most effective interventions to reduce relapse.
thinking: Chronic diarrhoea with weight loss ↓ Right iliac fossa pain and mass ↓ Young smoker ↓ Suggests terminal ileal inflammation ↓ Crohn's disease
exam_trap: C, Coeliac disease — chronic diarrhoea and weight loss fit, but it does not cause a right iliac fossa mass or localised pain after meals.
takeaway: Chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and a right iliac fossa mass in a young adult suggest Crohn's disease.

presentation: Coeliac disease associated with type 1 diabetes
stem:
A 16-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes since childhood is reviewed in the young person's diabetes clinic. Her mother reports months of loose stools and a bloated tummy, and she has dropped two centiles in weight. Her diabetes nurse has noticed unexplained hypoglycaemic episodes.

Which associated autoimmune condition should be tested for first?
why_correct: Coeliac disease is much more common in people with type 1 diabetes, and NICE recommends testing for it at diagnosis and when symptoms suggest it. Malabsorption causes diarrhoea, bloating and weight loss, and erratic carbohydrate absorption can cause unexplained hypoglycaemia. Coeliac serology should be checked while she is still eating gluten.
why_wrong: A. Addison's disease can cause hypoglycaemia and weight loss but does not explain chronic diarrhoea and bloating. B. Autoimmune hepatitis causes abnormal liver tests and jaundice rather than this picture. D. Pernicious anaemia causes B12 deficiency and is unusual at this age. E. Hypothyroidism is common in type 1 diabetes but causes weight gain and constipation rather than diarrhoea.
pearl: Coeliac disease is also more common in autoimmune thyroid disease, Down syndrome, Turner syndrome and in first-degree relatives of people with coeliac disease.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes ↓ Chronic diarrhoea, bloating and weight loss ↓ Unexplained hypoglycaemia suggests malabsorption ↓ Coeliac disease is a linked autoimmune condition ↓ Test coeliac serology while eating gluten
exam_trap: A, Addison's disease — it is associated with type 1 diabetes and causes hypoglycaemia and weight loss, but it does not explain months of diarrhoea and bloating.
takeaway: In type 1 diabetes, diarrhoea, weight loss or unexplained hypoglycaemia should prompt testing for coeliac disease.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman under investigation for months of abdominal pain, loose stools and weight loss has an ileocolonoscopy. The report describes deep ulcers in the terminal ileum and ascending colon with a cobblestone appearance, and normal mucosa between these areas; the rectum is spared. Biopsies show non-caseating granulomas.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Patchy inflammation with normal mucosa between affected segments (skip lesions), deep ulceration with cobblestoning, rectal sparing and non-caseating granulomas are characteristic of Crohn's disease. The inflammation is transmural and can affect any part of the gut from mouth to anus, most often the terminal ileum.
why_wrong: A. Ulcerative colitis causes continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum upwards, without skip lesions or granulomas. B. Intestinal tuberculosis can affect the ileocaecal region, but its granulomas are typically caseating. D. Microscopic colitis has normal-looking mucosa with changes only on histology. E. Coeliac disease affects the small bowel mucosa with villous atrophy, not colonic ulceration.
pearl: Transmural inflammation explains why Crohn's disease, unlike ulcerative colitis, causes strictures, fistulas and abscesses.
thinking: Chronic pain, diarrhoea and weight loss ↓ Patchy inflammation with normal areas between ↓ Cobblestoning and rectal sparing ↓ Non-caseating granulomas ↓ Crohn's disease
exam_trap: A, Ulcerative colitis — it is the other main inflammatory bowel disease, but it is continuous from the rectum and does not produce skip lesions or granulomas.
takeaway: Skip lesions with non-caseating granulomas on colonoscopy point to Crohn's disease.

stem:
A 27-year-old man was diagnosed with coeliac disease by duodenal biopsy a year ago. At his annual review he still has bloating and loose stools, and his tissue transglutaminase antibodies remain raised. He says he avoids bread at home but often has pasta, beer and takeaways with batter when out with friends.

What is the most important element of his management?

options.A: A course of oral prednisolone to settle the inflammation
options.C: Regular loperamide to control the diarrhoea
options.D: Strict, lifelong exclusion of gluten from his diet
options.E: Repeat duodenal biopsy before any change

correct_answer: D. Strict, lifelong exclusion of gluten from his diet
why_correct: The only effective treatment for coeliac disease is a strict, lifelong gluten-free diet. Persistently raised antibodies and ongoing symptoms in someone who regularly eats gluten point to dietary exposure rather than refractory disease. He should be referred to a dietitian for education about hidden sources of gluten such as beer, batter and sauces.
why_wrong: A. Steroids are only considered for proven refractory coeliac disease, which cannot be diagnosed while he is still eating gluten. B. Lactose avoidance may help temporarily but does not treat the underlying disease. C. Loperamide masks symptoms without stopping the damage to the gut. E. Repeat biopsy is reserved for persistent symptoms despite strict adherence; ongoing gluten intake is the obvious explanation here.
pearl: Ongoing gluten exposure is the commonest reason for persistent symptoms in coeliac disease; check adherence with a dietitian before considering refractory disease.
thinking: Established coeliac disease ↓ Ongoing symptoms and raised antibodies ↓ Frequent dietary gluten ↓ Non-adherence is the cause ↓ Strict lifelong gluten-free diet with dietitian support
exam_trap: E, Repeat duodenal biopsy — persistent symptoms seem to need investigation, but with clear ongoing gluten intake the priority is dietary adherence, not further tests.
takeaway: Coeliac disease is treated with a strict, lifelong gluten-free diet.

presentation: Crohn's disease affects mouth to anus
stem:
A 23-year-old man has had a painful perianal abscess drained twice in the past year. He now reports crops of painful ulcers inside his cheeks, intermittent loose stools and weight loss.

Which condition can involve any part of the gut from the mouth to the anus and best explains all his features?
why_correct: Crohn's disease can cause transmural inflammation anywhere from the mouth to the anus. Oral ulceration, perianal abscesses and fistulas, chronic diarrhoea and weight loss together strongly suggest it. He needs faecal calprotectin, bloods and referral to gastroenterology for ileocolonoscopy and imaging of the perianal region.
why_wrong: A. Ulcerative colitis is confined to the colon and does not typically cause recurrent perianal abscesses. B. Behçet's disease causes oral and genital ulcers but is a vasculitis rather than an inflammatory bowel disease and is a less likely explanation for perianal sepsis. C. Coeliac disease can cause mouth ulcers and diarrhoea but not perianal abscesses. D. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause ulcers, abscesses or weight loss.
pearl: Perianal disease such as skin tags, fissures, fistulas or abscesses is present in a substantial proportion of people with Crohn's disease and may come before gut symptoms.
thinking: Recurrent perianal abscesses ↓ Oral ulceration ↓ Chronic diarrhoea and weight loss ↓ Inflammation anywhere from mouth to anus ↓ Crohn's disease
exam_trap: A, Ulcerative colitis — it is the other common inflammatory bowel disease, but it is limited to the colon and does not explain oral and perianal disease.
takeaway: Oral ulcers, perianal disease and chronic diarrhoea together suggest Crohn's disease, which can affect the whole gut.
notes: Reviewer fix: Stem asked for an 'inflammatory bowel condition' but offered Behcet's/IBS/coeliac; reworded to 'Which condition' for homogeneous options

stem:
A 55-year-old woman with alcohol-related liver disease has an enlarged spleen and a low platelet count, and an ultrasound shows reversed flow in the portal vein. She is referred for an endoscopy to look for a serious consequence of her raised portal pressure.

Which complication is being screened for?
why_correct: Portal hypertension diverts blood through portosystemic collaterals, and at the gastro-oesophageal junction these form oesophageal and gastric varices. Varices can rupture and cause life-threatening haemorrhage, so people with cirrhosis are screened by upper GI endoscopy. Large varices are treated with a non-selective beta-blocker such as carvedilol or with band ligation.
why_wrong: A. Barrett's oesophagus is caused by chronic acid reflux, not raised portal pressure. B. Peptic ulcers are related to Helicobacter pylori and NSAIDs rather than portal hypertension. C. A Mallory–Weiss tear follows forceful vomiting and is not screened for. D. Candidiasis is linked to immunosuppression or inhaled steroids, not portal hypertension.
pearl: Suspected variceal bleeding should be treated with terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics before endoscopic band ligation.
thinking: Cirrhosis with splenomegaly and low platelets ↓ Reversed portal flow means portal hypertension ↓ Portosystemic collaterals form ↓ Oesophageal varices ↓ Screen with endoscopy to prevent bleeding
exam_trap: B, Peptic ulcer — it is a common cause of upper GI bleeding and is often found at endoscopy, but it is not caused by portal hypertension.
takeaway: Portal hypertension causes oesophageal varices, which people with cirrhosis are screened for by endoscopy.

stem:
A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis from long-standing hepatitis B asks his hepatology nurse why he has been told to attend regular liver scans for the rest of his life.

Which primary cancer of the liver is he at increased risk of?
why_correct: Cirrhosis of any cause is the main risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, and chronic hepatitis B adds further risk. Regenerating nodules in a cirrhotic liver can undergo malignant change. Surveillance aims to detect small tumours that are still suitable for curative treatment.
why_wrong: A. Cholangiocarcinoma is linked to primary sclerosing cholangitis and is much less common than hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhosis. B. Hepatoblastoma is a cancer of young children. D. Haemangioma is a common benign lesion, not a cancer. E. Metastases are secondary tumours and cirrhosis does not increase the risk of them.
pearl: Hepatitis B can cause hepatocellular carcinoma even without cirrhosis, so some people with hepatitis B are offered surveillance before cirrhosis develops.
thinking: Cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis B ↓ Nodular regeneration and chronic inflammation ↓ High risk of primary liver cancer ↓ Hepatocellular carcinoma ↓ Surveillance to find early tumours
exam_trap: A, Cholangiocarcinoma — it is a primary liver cancer, but it is mainly linked to biliary disease and is far less common in cirrhosis than hepatocellular carcinoma.
takeaway: Cirrhosis, especially from viral hepatitis, is the main risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma.

stem:
A 57-year-old woman with compensated cirrhosis due to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) has been told she will need lifelong checks for liver cancer. She asks her GP what kind of scan will be used each time.

What is the usual imaging for this surveillance in the UK?

options.A: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis

why_correct: NICE recommends ultrasound of the liver, with or without serum alpha-fetoprotein, every six months for hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance in people with cirrhosis. Ultrasound is safe, widely available and avoids radiation. A new nodule is then assessed with contrast-enhanced CT or MRI.
why_wrong: A. CT involves radiation and contrast and is used to characterise lesions, not for routine surveillance. B. PET-CT is not sensitive for most hepatocellular carcinomas and is not used for surveillance. D. Plain X-ray cannot show liver lesions. E. Transient elastography measures liver stiffness to assess fibrosis, not to detect tumours.
pearl: Surveillance is only worthwhile for people who would be fit enough to be treated if a cancer were found.
thinking: Cirrhosis ↓ High risk of hepatocellular carcinoma ↓ Needs safe, repeatable imaging ↓ Six-monthly liver ultrasound ↓ CT or MRI only to characterise new nodules
exam_trap: E, Transient elastography — it is a liver scan done often in cirrhosis, but it measures stiffness and fibrosis rather than detecting tumours.
takeaway: Hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance in cirrhosis is with six-monthly liver ultrasound.
notes: Reviewer fix: Updated outdated term 'metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease' to MASLD (steatotic) nomenclature

stem:
A 58-year-old woman with alcohol-related liver disease has medium-sized oesophageal varices seen at a surveillance endoscopy. They have never bled. The hepatology nurse starts her on carvedilol and she asks how this tablet will protect her.

What is the main mechanism of benefit?

options.A: It lowers pressure in the portal venous system
options.B: It thickens the oesophageal mucosa over the varices
options.C: It increases clotting factor production by the liver
options.D: It reduces gastric acid that erodes the varices
options.E: It speeds the heart to improve hepatic blood flow

correct_answer: A. It lowers pressure in the portal venous system
why_correct: Carvedilol and propranolol are non-selective beta-blockers that reduce portal pressure by lowering cardiac output (beta-1 blockade) and causing splanchnic vasoconstriction (unopposed alpha tone after beta-2 blockade). Lower portal pressure reduces tension in the variceal wall and so lowers the risk of a first bleed. This is why they are used as primary prophylaxis for medium or large varices.
why_wrong: B. Beta-blockers have no effect on the structure of the oesophageal lining. C. They do not improve hepatic synthetic function or clotting factor production. D. Acid suppression is the role of a proton pump inhibitor, not a beta-blocker. E. Beta-blockers slow the heart and reduce, rather than increase, splanchnic inflow.
pearl: Carvedilol is favoured by BSG and Baveno VII guidance for primary prevention of variceal bleeding because its added alpha-1 blockade lowers portal pressure more than propranolol; endoscopic band ligation is the alternative (and the NICE-recommended option) for medium to large varices.
thinking: Cirrhosis with varices that have not bled ↓ Goal is primary prevention of haemorrhage ↓ Variceal bleeding risk rises with portal pressure ↓ Non-selective beta-blockade lowers cardiac output and splanchnic inflow ↓ Portal pressure falls
exam_trap: D, Reducing gastric acid — acid suppression feels intuitive for any upper GI bleeding risk, but it is the job of a PPI and is not how beta-blockers protect varices.
takeaway: Non-selective beta-blockers prevent variceal bleeding by reducing portal hypertension.
notes: Reviewer fix: Pearl said carvedilol 'now the preferred' option; reworded to BSG/Baveno VII preference and noted band ligation as the alternative (NICE CG141 recommends VBL for medium/large varices).

stem:
On a gastroenterology ward round, a 66-year-old woman with known liver cirrhosis seems slower to answer questions than yesterday. The registrar asks her to hold both arms out straight with her hands cocked back. Her hands repeatedly drop forward and then jerk back up, irregularly.

Which term describes this sign?
why_correct: This is asterixis: brief, irregular lapses of the muscle tone holding a posture, so the dorsiflexed hands drop and are then pulled back. It is a negative myoclonus and, in a patient with cirrhosis who is becoming slowed, is a classic sign of hepatic encephalopathy. It can also occur in uraemia and carbon dioxide retention.
why_wrong: A. Intention tremor appears on reaching for a target and suggests cerebellar disease. C. Chorea is a flowing, dance-like movement not provoked by holding a posture. D. Fasciculations are small visible twitches of muscle fibres, typical of lower motor neurone disease. E. A pill-rolling tremor is a regular rhythmic tremor at rest that lessens with voluntary movement, not an irregular lapse of a held posture.
pearl: Asterixis is not specific to liver failure: it is also seen in type 2 respiratory failure with hypercapnia and in advanced kidney failure.
thinking: Cirrhosis with new slowing of thought ↓ Sign elicited by holding the wrists extended ↓ Hands lapse forward then correct ↓ Loss of postural tone, not an active tremor ↓ Asterixis, pointing to hepatic encephalopathy
exam_trap: A, Intention tremor — any coarse hand movement tempts a tremor label, but intention tremor needs goal-directed movement, whereas asterixis appears when a posture is held.
takeaway: A flapping lapse of posture in outstretched, extended hands is asterixis, a key sign of hepatic encephalopathy.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_wrong E: pill-rolling tremor described as settling with posture; corrected to rest tremor that lessens with voluntary movement.

stem:
A 70-year-old man with cirrhosis is brought to the emergency department by his wife, who says he has been muddled and sleepy for two days. She mentions he has not opened his bowels for almost a week. He has a flap of the outstretched hands. His other history includes knee osteoarthritis, glaucoma treated with eye drops and long-standing tinnitus.

Which item in his history is the most likely trigger for his deterioration?
why_correct: Constipation increases the time colonic bacteria have to produce ammonia and other nitrogenous toxins, which a cirrhotic liver cannot clear, so it is a classic trigger of hepatic encephalopathy. His confusion, drowsiness and asterixis fit that diagnosis. Treatment includes lactulose titrated to two or three soft stools a day, while also looking for infection, bleeding, electrolyte disturbance and sedative drugs.
why_wrong: B. Osteoarthritis does not alter ammonia handling, although sedating analgesics given for it could. C. Topical glaucoma drops are not a recognised trigger. D. Tinnitus has no link with liver failure. E. Age alone does not explain an acute decline over two days.
pearl: Common precipitants of hepatic encephalopathy include constipation, infection (including spontaneous bacterial peritonitis), gastrointestinal bleeding, hypokalaemia, dehydration and sedatives such as benzodiazepines or opioids.
thinking: Cirrhosis with acute confusion and drowsiness ↓ Asterixis suggests hepatic encephalopathy ↓ Look for a precipitant ↓ Nearly a week without bowel opening ↓ Constipation raises gut ammonia load, so treat with lactulose
exam_trap: B, Knee osteoarthritis — chronic pain conditions can lead to sedative drug use, but the osteoarthritis itself is not a trigger, whereas the constipation is directly causal.
takeaway: In cirrhosis with new confusion, constipation is a common and easily reversible trigger of hepatic encephalopathy.

stem:
A 68-year-old woman phones NHS 111 because she has not passed a stool for five days and feels bloated with griping lower abdominal pains. She is passing wind and has not vomited. Ten days ago, after a hip fracture repair, she was discharged on regular codeine. Before the operation her bowels opened daily.

What is the most likely explanation?
correct_answer: A. Constipation caused by the opioid
why_correct: Opioids such as codeine act on mu receptors in the gut wall, slowing transit and increasing fluid absorption, so hard stools and bloating are very common. The timing here, with a previously normal bowel habit and symptoms starting after regular codeine, makes this the likely cause. She is still passing wind and not vomiting, which is reassuring against obstruction, and a laxative should be co-prescribed with any regular opioid.
why_wrong: B. New irritable bowel syndrome in later life is unlikely and would not explain the clear link to a new drug. C. Crohn's disease usually causes diarrhoea, pain and weight loss rather than constipation. D. Cholecystitis causes right upper quadrant pain and fever. E. Lactose intolerance causes loose stools and wind after dairy, not hard stools.
pearl: When regular opioids are started, prescribe a stimulant laxative (with or without a softener) at the same time; bulk-forming laxatives are generally avoided because they can worsen opioid-related constipation.
thinking: Older woman with new constipation and bloating ↓ Bowel habit was normal until recently ↓ Regular codeine started after surgery ↓ Still passing flatus, no vomiting ↓ Opioid-induced constipation
exam_trap: B, New irritable bowel syndrome — bloating and cramping fit IBS, but new symptoms in later life with a clear drug trigger point to the opioid instead.
takeaway: New constipation soon after starting a regular opioid is most likely drug-induced and is best prevented by co-prescribing a laxative.

stem:
A 36-year-old office worker sees the practice nurse about passing hard stools only two or three times a week for several months. She has no weight loss or rectal bleeding. She eats mainly white bread and ready meals, rarely has fruit, and drinks little apart from coffee during the working day.

Which advice is most likely to help her bowel habit?

options.A: Cut out fruit to reduce wind and bloating
options.B: Take a daily enema as a first step
options.C: Increase dietary fibre gradually and drink more fluid
options.D: Skip breakfast to rest the bowel
options.E: Restrict fluids to concentrate the stool

correct_answer: C. Increase dietary fibre gradually and drink more fluid
why_correct: First-line management of chronic constipation without red flags is lifestyle change: a gradual rise in dietary fibre from wholegrains, fruit and vegetables, adequate fluid intake and regular activity. Her low-fibre diet and poor fluid intake are likely contributors. If this is not enough, a bulk-forming laxative such as ispaghula is the usual next step.
why_wrong: A. Fruit is a useful source of fibre, so cutting it out would worsen constipation. B. Enemas are not first-line for chronic constipation and are not used daily. D. Missing meals removes the gastrocolic reflex that helps bowel opening after eating. E. Fluid restriction makes stools harder.
pearl: Fibre should be increased gradually over several weeks, as a sudden rise often causes bloating and wind that make people give up.
thinking: Chronic hard, infrequent stools ↓ No red flag features ↓ Low-fibre diet and poor fluid intake ↓ Lifestyle measures come first ↓ More fibre and fluid, then a bulk-forming laxative if needed
exam_trap: A, Cutting out fruit — it sounds sensible if she feels bloated, but it removes fibre and makes constipation worse.
takeaway: In uncomplicated chronic constipation, start by gradually increasing fibre and fluid before turning to laxatives.

stem:
A 74-year-old woman is seen in the GP surgery after her daughter noticed her eyes looked yellow. Over the past fortnight her urine has become the colour of strong tea and her stools now look pale and putty-like. Her skin is itchy.

What does this combination of findings indicate?
correct_answer: B. Blockage of bile flow (obstructive jaundice)
why_correct: Dark urine and pale stools mean conjugated bilirubin is reaching the blood and being filtered by the kidneys, while too little bile is reaching the gut to colour the stool. Itch from retained bile salts adds to this picture of cholestasis. In an older person, obstructive jaundice, particularly if painless, should prompt urgent investigation, including ultrasound, for causes such as pancreatic or biliary cancer.
why_wrong: A. Haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin, which does not enter urine, and stools are normal or dark. C. Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with normal urine and stools. D. Dehydration can darken urine but does not cause jaundice or pale stools. E. Carotenaemia yellows the skin but spares the sclerae and does not alter urine or stools.
pearl: Under NICE suspected cancer guidance, adults aged 40 and over with jaundice should be referred on a suspected cancer pathway for possible pancreatic cancer.
thinking: Yellow sclerae ↓ Dark urine means conjugated bilirubin in the blood ↓ Pale stools mean bile is not reaching the gut ↓ Itch from retained bile salts ↓ Cholestatic or obstructive jaundice
exam_trap: A, Haemolytic anaemia — haemolysis also causes jaundice, but the bilirubin is unconjugated, so urine stays normal coloured and stools are not pale.
takeaway: Jaundice with dark urine, pale stools and itch points to obstruction of bile flow.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_correct called the jaundice 'painless' though the stem does not state this; reworded to 'particularly if painless'.

presentation: Coeliac serology on a gluten-containing diet
stem:
A 25-year-old man attends the GP surgery with bloating and loose stools. His sister has coeliac disease, and two weeks ago he cut out bread, pasta and cereals, which has helped. The GP wants to check whether he has coeliac disease.

What should he be advised before the blood test?

options.A: Stay gluten-free so the test is done while he feels well
options.B: Go straight to a duodenal biopsy instead of a blood test
options.C: Reintroduce gluten in more than one meal every day for at least 6 weeks before testing
options.D: Have the test now, as his partial gluten exclusion will not matter
options.E: Avoid testing because his response to the diet confirms the diagnosis

correct_answer: C. Reintroduce gluten in more than one meal every day for at least 6 weeks before testing
why_correct: Coeliac serology and duodenal histology only become abnormal while gluten is being eaten, so a gluten-free or reduced-gluten diet can give false-negative results. NICE advises eating gluten in more than one meal every day for at least 6 weeks before testing. A symptomatic response to gluten avoidance does not confirm coeliac disease, and a formal diagnosis matters for follow-up and family screening.
why_wrong: A. Testing while gluten-free risks a falsely negative result. B. Biopsy is also unreliable without gluten intake and is normally arranged after positive serology. D. Even partial gluten exclusion can lower antibody levels and cause a false negative. E. Improvement on a gluten-free diet is non-specific and is not diagnostic.
pearl: First-degree relatives of people with coeliac disease have a much higher risk than the general population and should be offered serological testing.
thinking: Symptoms suggestive of coeliac disease ↓ Has already cut out gluten ↓ Serology and biopsy need ongoing gluten exposure ↓ False negative risk if tested now ↓ Reintroduce gluten daily for a period, then test
exam_trap: A, Staying gluten-free — it seems kind as he feels better, but it makes the test unreliable and may miss the diagnosis.
takeaway: Test for coeliac disease only while the person is eating gluten regularly.

stem:
A 64-year-old woman who takes a proton pump inhibitor and regular ibuprofen for back pain has had several months of frequent watery stools, sometimes waking her at night, with no blood. At colonoscopy the bowel lining looks entirely normal, but random biopsies taken along the colon show a thickened subepithelial collagen band.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Microscopic colitis causes chronic, watery, non-bloody diarrhoea in older people, often women, with a normal-looking colon; the diagnosis is made only on histology. A thickened collagen band defines the collagenous subtype. Drugs such as NSAIDs and proton pump inhibitors are recognised associations and should be reviewed, and budesonide is the usual treatment.
why_wrong: A. Irritable bowel syndrome is a diagnosis with normal biopsies and does not usually cause nocturnal diarrhoea. B. Coeliac disease is diagnosed on duodenal, not colonic, biopsy. D. Ulcerative colitis causes bloody diarrhoea with visible mucosal inflammation. E. Bile acid diarrhoea leaves the colonic histology normal.
pearl: Always take random colonic biopsies when colonoscopy is done for chronic diarrhoea, even if the mucosa looks normal, or microscopic colitis will be missed.
thinking: Chronic watery diarrhoea in an older woman ↓ Nocturnal symptoms suggest an organic cause ↓ Normal-looking colon at colonoscopy ↓ Biopsies show a thickened collagen band ↓ Collagenous microscopic colitis
exam_trap: A, Irritable bowel syndrome — a normal colonoscopy tempts a functional label, but abnormal histology and night-time diarrhoea point to an organic cause.
takeaway: Watery diarrhoea with a normal colon but abnormal colonic biopsies is microscopic colitis.

stem:
A 29-year-old man books an urgent GP appointment with three weeks of loose, greasy stools, wind and cramping that have not settled. He came back a month ago from a trekking holiday in Nepal.

Which further question is most important to ask?

options.A: Whether he has a family history of bowel cancer
options.B: What he ate and drank on the trip, including untreated water
options.C: Whether he has any recent joint stiffness
options.D: How much exercise he takes each week
options.E: Whether he has ever had hay fever

correct_answer: B. What he ate and drank on the trip, including untreated water
why_correct: Persistent diarrhoea after travel to a low-income region raises the possibility of an infection such as giardiasis, amoebiasis or bacterial enteritis. Asking about drinking water, street food, ice and contacts helps judge the likely organism and guides stool testing, including requesting ova, cysts and parasites. Greasy stools and wind after drinking from streams would particularly suggest Giardia.
why_wrong: A. Family history of bowel cancer matters for chronic symptoms in older people but does not address the clear travel link. C. Joint stiffness is not the most useful lead here. D. Exercise habits do not help identify the cause. E. Hay fever is irrelevant to post-travel diarrhoea.
pearl: When requesting stool tests after foreign travel, include the travel destination on the form so the laboratory can look for parasites such as Giardia and Entamoeba.
thinking: Persistent diarrhoea after a trip abroad ↓ Infection is the leading concern ↓ Exposure history shapes the likely organism ↓ Ask about water, food and contacts ↓ Guide stool microscopy and culture
exam_trap: A, Family history of bowel cancer — a sensible question in many bowel histories, but here the timing after trekking makes travel exposure the key line of enquiry.
takeaway: In diarrhoea after travel, a detailed food and water exposure history is essential.

stem:
A 41-year-old man has had several months of loose stools with bloating. His GP suspects irritable bowel syndrome.

Which additional finding would most strongly point away from IBS and towards an organic cause?

options.A: Pain that settles after opening his bowels
options.B: Bloating that worsens through the day
options.C: Stools that alternate between loose and hard

why_correct: Unexplained weight loss is an alarm feature that is not part of IBS and should prompt assessment for organic disease such as inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease or colorectal cancer. Pain relieved by defaecation, bloating, variable stool form and post-prandial worsening are all typical of IBS. A diagnosis of IBS should only be made when red flags are absent.
why_wrong: A. Pain eased by defaecation is a core feature of IBS. B. Bloating that builds during the day is common in IBS. C. Alternating stool form fits mixed-type IBS. D. Worsening after meals is common in IBS.
pearl: Other red flags that should prevent a diagnosis of IBS include rectal bleeding, a family history of bowel or ovarian cancer, anaemia, a raised inflammatory marker and new symptoms in people over 60.
thinking: Chronic loose stools and bloating ↓ IBS is suspected ↓ Look for alarm features before labelling ↓ Unintentional weight loss is not part of IBS ↓ Investigate for organic disease
exam_trap: D, Symptoms after eating — meal-related symptoms can feel worrying, but they are common in IBS and do not on their own suggest organic disease.
takeaway: Unexplained weight loss is a red flag that should stop a clinician labelling bowel symptoms as IBS.

stem:
A care home nurse asks the visiting GP for advice about an 82-year-old resident who has had frequent loose stools for a week while recovering from an infection. The skin around her anus is now red and sore but not broken.

What is the most appropriate skin care?

options.A: Wash the area with neat antiseptic after each stool
options.B: Rub the area firmly with scented wet wipes
options.C: Clean gently with water, pat dry and apply a barrier cream
options.D: Restrict her drinks to make the stool firmer
options.E: Leave the area unwashed between baths to avoid friction

correct_answer: C. Clean gently with water, pat dry and apply a barrier cream
why_correct: Frequent contact with liquid stool causes irritant dermatitis. Gentle cleansing with warm water or a pH-balanced cleanser, patting rather than rubbing dry, and applying a barrier cream protects the skin from further damage. The cause of the diarrhoea should also be addressed and her hydration maintained.
why_wrong: A. Concentrated antiseptics strip the skin and worsen irritation. B. Vigorous rubbing and fragranced wipes cause friction and contact irritation. D. Fluid restriction risks dehydration and does not treat the skin. E. Leaving stool on the skin prolongs exposure to irritants.
pearl: Moisture-associated skin damage from incontinence can progress to breakdown and pressure ulcers, so early barrier protection is an important part of nursing care in frail adults.
thinking: Frail resident with ongoing loose stools ↓ Red, intact perianal skin ↓ Irritant dermatitis from stool contact ↓ Reduce friction and irritants ↓ Gentle cleansing and barrier cream
exam_trap: A, Neat antiseptic — it sounds hygienic, but strong antiseptics damage already irritated skin.
takeaway: Protect perianal skin in diarrhoea with gentle cleansing and a barrier cream.

stem:
A 23-year-old woman sees her GP with two months of loose stools mixed with blood and mucus. She has to rush to the toilet several times a day and has crampy lower abdominal pain. Stool cultures arranged earlier were negative.

Which group of conditions is most likely?
why_correct: Weeks of bloody diarrhoea with mucus, urgency and cramping in a young adult, with infection excluded by negative cultures, strongly suggest inflammatory bowel disease, most likely ulcerative colitis. Faecal calprotectin and blood tests support the assessment, and she needs referral for colonoscopy and biopsy. Severity should be assessed, as frequent bloody stools with systemic features need same-day hospital review.
why_wrong: A. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause blood in the stool. B. Haemorrhoids cause bright red blood on the paper, not blood mixed into diarrhoea. D. Microscopic colitis causes watery, non-bloody diarrhoea, mostly in older people. E. Diverticular disease is unusual at this age and does not cause weeks of bloody diarrhoea with urgency.
pearl: Always send stool cultures, including for Clostridioides difficile where relevant, before attributing bloody diarrhoea to inflammatory bowel disease.
thinking: Young adult with weeks of bloody diarrhoea ↓ Urgency and mucus suggest rectal inflammation ↓ Stool cultures negative ↓ Persistent inflammatory colitis ↓ Inflammatory bowel disease, likely ulcerative colitis
exam_trap: B, Haemorrhoids — they are a common cause of rectal bleeding, but they do not cause diarrhoea with blood mixed in, urgency and cramps.
takeaway: Persistent bloody diarrhoea with urgency in a young adult suggests inflammatory bowel disease once infection is excluded.

stem:
A 38-year-old man attends a fracture clinic after breaking his wrist in a minor fall. He mentions bulky, pale, loose stools for over a year and his trousers have become loose. Blood tests show a low serum calcium, low vitamin D and a raised alkaline phosphatase.

Which underlying process best explains these findings?
why_correct: Long-standing pale, bulky stools and weight loss suggest fat malabsorption. Vitamin D is fat-soluble and calcium absorption depends on it, so malabsorption leads to low calcium and vitamin D with a raised alkaline phosphatase, the picture of osteomalacia, and fragility fractures. Coeliac disease is a common underlying cause and should be tested for.
why_wrong: B. Primary hyperparathyroidism causes high, not low, calcium. C. Hyperthyroidism can cause loose stools and bone loss but does not cause low calcium and vitamin D or steatorrhoea. D. Cushing syndrome causes osteoporosis with weight gain, not steatorrhoea. E. Diabetes insipidus causes thirst and large urine volumes.
pearl: Osteomalacia gives low or low-normal calcium and phosphate with a raised alkaline phosphatase, whereas osteoporosis typically has normal bone biochemistry.
thinking: Chronic pale, bulky stools and weight loss ↓ Suggests fat malabsorption ↓ Low vitamin D and calcium, raised ALP ↓ Osteomalacia with fragility fracture ↓ Underlying malabsorption, such as coeliac disease
exam_trap: B, Primary hyperparathyroidism — it is a classic cause of bone disease, but it raises calcium, whereas this man has low calcium.
takeaway: Steatorrhoea with low calcium and vitamin D suggests malabsorption causing osteomalacia.

stem:
A 20-year-old university athlete has been tired for some months and has lost weight. She describes recurrent crampy abdominal pain and loose stools. Her father has Crohn's disease. Her GP wants a non-invasive test that best helps decide between inflammatory bowel disease and a functional bowel disorder.

Which test is most appropriate?
why_correct: Calprotectin is released by neutrophils into the bowel lumen, so a raised faecal level indicates intestinal inflammation. NICE recommends it in primary care to help distinguish inflammatory bowel disease from irritable bowel syndrome in adults with recent-onset lower GI symptoms when cancer is not suspected. Her weight loss and family history make IBD a real concern, so a raised result would support referral for colonoscopy.
why_wrong: A. Amylase is used for acute pancreatitis. B. Faecal elastase assesses pancreatic exocrine function, not gut inflammation. C. Thyroid tests may be part of a diarrhoea work-up but do not separate IBD from functional disorders. D. The faecal immunochemical test detects blood and is used mainly to assess colorectal cancer risk.
pearl: Faecal calprotectin can be falsely raised by NSAIDs, gastrointestinal infection and colorectal cancer, so it must be interpreted with the clinical picture.
thinking: Young adult with chronic loose stools and pain ↓ Weight loss and family history of Crohn's disease ↓ Need to separate inflammation from a functional disorder ↓ Neutrophil protein in stool marks gut inflammation ↓ Faecal calprotectin
exam_trap: D, Faecal immunochemical test — it is a stool test used in bowel symptoms, but it detects blood for cancer risk and does not measure inflammation.
takeaway: Faecal calprotectin is the key non-invasive test to separate inflammatory bowel disease from IBS.

stem:
A 46-year-old teacher returns to the GP for results. For five months she has had episodes of watery motions, mostly first thing in the morning, which come in bursts around stressful school terms. Nothing has woken her at night, there has been no blood, and her weight is unchanged. Her blood count, CRP, coeliac antibody test and faecal calprotectin are all within normal limits.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Months of intermittent loose stools linked to stress, with no nocturnal symptoms, weight loss or bleeding, and normal blood tests, coeliac serology and faecal calprotectin fits irritable bowel syndrome. A normal calprotectin makes active inflammatory bowel disease unlikely. IBS can be diagnosed positively in this situation without further invasive tests.
why_wrong: B. Active Crohn's disease would usually raise faecal calprotectin and often causes weight loss. C. Colorectal cancer is unlikely without bleeding, anaemia or weight loss. D. Infective colitis is an acute illness rather than five months of symptoms. E. Ulcerative colitis usually causes bloody diarrhoea with a raised calprotectin.
pearl: IBS should be diagnosed positively on symptoms plus normal baseline tests, rather than only after exhaustive exclusion of every other cause.
thinking: Months of intermittent loose stools ↓ Stress-related, no night-time symptoms ↓ No weight loss, bleeding or anaemia ↓ Normal inflammatory markers, coeliac serology and calprotectin ↓ Irritable bowel syndrome
exam_trap: B, Crohn's disease — months of loose stools can suggest IBD, but a normal faecal calprotectin with no alarm features makes active inflammation unlikely.
takeaway: Chronic bowel symptoms with no red flags and a normal faecal calprotectin are most consistent with IBS.

stem:
A 29-year-old man who recently moved to the UK from East Asia notices wind, gurgling and loose stools within a couple of hours of drinking milky tea. He is otherwise well. His GP explains that he is probably not digesting the sugar in milk.

A shortage of which enzyme is responsible?
why_correct: Lactase sits on the brush border of the small intestine and splits lactose into glucose and galactose. When it is deficient, undigested lactose reaches the colon, draws in water osmotically and is fermented by bacteria, producing gas and loose stools. Primary lactase decline after childhood is very common in people of East Asian and African heritage.
why_wrong: A. Sucrase splits sucrose, the sugar in table sugar, not milk sugar. C. Lipase breaks down dietary fat. D. Trypsin is a pancreatic protease. E. Amylase digests starch.
pearl: Secondary lactase deficiency can follow damage to the small bowel lining, for example after gastroenteritis or in untreated coeliac disease, and often improves as the mucosa heals.
thinking: Wind and loose stools after milk ↓ Milk sugar is lactose ↓ Lactose is split by a brush-border enzyme ↓ Undigested lactose causes osmotic diarrhoea and fermentation ↓ Lactase deficiency
exam_trap: A, Sucrase — another brush-border disaccharidase, but it acts on sucrose, not the lactose in milk.
takeaway: Lactose intolerance results from deficiency of the brush-border enzyme lactase.

stem:
A 27-year-old woman calls NHS 111 after a day of repeated vomiting and frequent watery stools that began after a takeaway meal. She feels very thirsty, a little light-headed when she stands, and has passed only a small amount of dark urine since the morning.

Which complication is she most likely to have developed?
why_correct: Vomiting and diarrhoea cause loss of water and electrolytes, and thirst, postural light-headedness and reduced dark urine are features of dehydration. She needs oral rehydration if she can keep fluids down, or assessment for intravenous fluids if she cannot. Warning signs such as confusion, very little urine or persistent vomiting should prompt urgent review.
why_wrong: A. Acute pancreatitis causes severe epigastric pain radiating to the back rather than diarrhoea after food. B. Hypothyroidism is a chronic condition unrelated to acute fluid loss. C. Diabetic ketoacidosis can cause vomiting and thirst, but there is no history of diabetes and diarrhoea after a meal points to gastroenteritis. D. Bowel obstruction causes constipation and distension, not frequent watery stools.
pearl: Oral rehydration solution replaces sodium and glucose together, using the sodium-glucose co-transporter to drive water absorption even when the gut is inflamed.
thinking: Acute vomiting and watery stools after a meal ↓ Large fluid and electrolyte losses ↓ Thirst and postural light-headedness ↓ Small volumes of dark urine ↓ Dehydration
exam_trap: C, Diabetic ketoacidosis — thirst and vomiting are features of DKA, but without known diabetes, and with diarrhoea after a takeaway, simple fluid loss is far more likely.
takeaway: Thirst, postural symptoms and reduced urine after vomiting and diarrhoea indicate dehydration.

stem:
A 47-year-old man had a duodenal biopsy that confirmed coeliac disease after positive blood tests. At follow-up with the dietitian he asks which part of his diet he will need to exclude for life.

What should he be told to avoid?

options.E: Gluten-containing foods such as wheat, barley and rye

correct_answer: E. Gluten-containing foods such as wheat, barley and rye
why_correct: Coeliac disease is an immune reaction to gluten, found in wheat, barley and rye, so the only effective treatment is a strict lifelong gluten-free diet. This allows the small bowel lining to heal and reduces long-term risks such as osteoporosis and small bowel lymphoma. Oats are tolerated by most people if they are uncontaminated.
why_wrong: A. Some people have temporary lactose intolerance at diagnosis, but dairy does not need lifelong exclusion. B. Fat restriction is not part of coeliac treatment. C. Fruit sugars are not a trigger. D. Fibre does not need to be avoided.
pearl: People with coeliac disease should be offered an annual review, including checking diet adherence, symptoms, weight and a blood count.
thinking: Coeliac disease confirmed by serology and biopsy ↓ Immune reaction to gluten ↓ Gluten in wheat, barley and rye ↓ Removing the trigger lets the mucosa heal ↓ Lifelong gluten-free diet
exam_trap: A, All dairy products — lactose intolerance can coexist at diagnosis, but it is usually temporary and dairy is not the cause of coeliac disease.
takeaway: Coeliac disease is treated with lifelong strict avoidance of gluten.

stem:
A 16-year-old girl recently diagnosed with coeliac disease is reviewed in the paediatric clinic with her mother. She feels well now and wants to know why she cannot have the occasional slice of pizza with friends.

Which explanation is correct?

options.A: Gluten provokes an immune reaction that damages the lining of the small intestine
options.B: Gluten causes an IgE-mediated allergic reaction like a nut allergy
options.C: Gluten is a direct toxin to the liver
options.D: Gluten cannot be broken down because her pancreas is not working
options.E: Gluten causes overgrowth of bacteria in the large bowel

correct_answer: A. Gluten provokes an immune reaction that damages the lining of the small intestine
why_correct: In coeliac disease, gluten peptides are modified by tissue transglutaminase and presented by HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 molecules, triggering a T-cell response that causes villous atrophy in the small bowel. This damage can occur even after small amounts of gluten and even when there are no symptoms. Ongoing exposure increases the risk of anaemia, osteoporosis, poor growth and small bowel lymphoma.
why_wrong: B. An IgE-mediated reaction describes wheat allergy, a different condition with rapid allergic symptoms. C. Coeliac disease is not a direct liver toxicity, although liver enzymes can be mildly raised. D. Pancreatic function is normal in coeliac disease. E. The process occurs in the small intestine, not through colonic bacterial overgrowth.
pearl: Almost everyone with coeliac disease carries HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8, so a negative HLA test makes the diagnosis very unlikely.
thinking: Teenager with confirmed coeliac disease ↓ Asks why small amounts matter ↓ Gluten drives a T-cell immune reaction ↓ Villous atrophy in the small bowel even without symptoms ↓ Strict avoidance is needed
exam_trap: B, An IgE-mediated allergy — the word allergy is often used loosely, but coeliac disease is a T-cell immune enteropathy, not an IgE reaction.
takeaway: Gluten in coeliac disease causes immune-mediated damage to the small bowel, even when symptoms are absent.

stem:
A 49-year-old bus driver has had gnawing upper abdominal pain that wakes him at night and is relieved by eating. He takes no anti-inflammatory drugs. Endoscopy shows an ulcer in the first part of the duodenum.

Which organism is most likely to be responsible?
why_correct: Helicobacter pylori is the most common cause of duodenal ulcers, particularly in people not taking NSAIDs. It colonises the gastric antrum and increases acid secretion, damaging the duodenal mucosa. He should be tested for H. pylori and, if positive, given eradication therapy with a proton pump inhibitor and two antibiotics.
why_wrong: A. Campylobacter causes acute infective diarrhoea. C. E. coli causes gastroenteritis and urinary infections, not peptic ulcers. D. Hepatitis B affects the liver. E. C. difficile causes colitis, usually after antibiotics.
pearl: Pain from a duodenal ulcer is classically eased by eating, whereas pain from a gastric ulcer is often made worse by food.
thinking: Nocturnal epigastric pain relieved by food ↓ Duodenal ulcer seen at endoscopy ↓ No NSAID use ↓ Most common cause is gastric bacterial infection ↓ Helicobacter pylori
exam_trap: A, Campylobacter jejuni — it is a curved gut bacterium like H. pylori, but it causes acute enteritis, not peptic ulceration.
takeaway: Helicobacter pylori is the main cause of duodenal ulcers in people not taking NSAIDs.

presentation: Upper GI cancer red flags in dyspepsia
stem:
A 51-year-old bus driver sees his GP about six weeks of a full, uncomfortable feeling high in his abdomen that comes on after only a few mouthfuls of food. Examination is unremarkable. The GP goes through a list of further questions.

Which additional symptom, if he reported it, would most justify referral on a suspected cancer pathway for oesophageal or stomach cancer?

options.B: Food sticking on the way down when he swallows
options.C: Burning pain that settles quickly with an over-the-counter antacid
options.D: Abdominal bloating that builds through the evening
options.E: Heartburn after a large late-night meal

correct_answer: B. Food sticking on the way down when he swallows
why_correct: Dysphagia is a red-flag symptom for oesophageal and gastric cancer. NICE suspected cancer guidance recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral for anyone with dysphagia, whatever their age. Adding it to his early satiety and upper abdominal discomfort would change management from treating dyspepsia to urgent specialist assessment.
why_wrong: A. Belching is a common, non-specific dyspeptic symptom. C. Prompt relief with antacids points to acid-related symptoms rather than an alarm feature. D. Evening bloating is a functional-type symptom with no alarm value. E. Heartburn after a heavy meal suggests reflux and, on its own, does not mandate a cancer referral.
pearl: In uninvestigated dyspepsia without alarm features, NICE advises a full-dose PPI for a month or test and treat for Helicobacter pylori, but any dysphagia moves the patient straight to the suspected cancer pathway.
thinking: Dyspepsia with early satiety in a middle-aged man ↓ Most such symptoms are benign ↓ Look for red flags that change the pathway ↓ Dysphagia is a red flag at any age ↓ Suspected cancer pathway referral
exam_trap: E, Heartburn after a large meal — it sounds like an upper GI symptom worth acting on, but it is typical reflux and does not by itself warrant a cancer referral.
takeaway: Any dysphagia in a patient with dyspepsia warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral, regardless of age.

stem:
Following a year of food and drinks lodging behind her sternum, a 39-year-old graphic designer has had a normal upper GI endoscopy. Oesophageal manometry has now been performed in the hospital gastroenterology unit. It shows absent peristalsis in the body of the oesophagus and incomplete relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter with each swallow.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Manometry is the diagnostic test for achalasia, and the combination of absent oesophageal body peristalsis with a lower oesophageal sphincter that fails to relax on swallowing is its hallmark.
