Her symptoms with both food and fluids and the normal endoscopy fit a motility problem rather than a structural lesion.
why_wrong: A. A peptic stricture is a structural narrowing that would be seen at endoscopy and does not abolish peristalsis. B. Adenocarcinoma would be visible at endoscopy and biopsy; malignant infiltration of the cardia can mimic achalasia but is excluded here. D. Diffuse oesophageal spasm shows premature, uncoordinated contractions with normal sphincter relaxation. E. Eosinophilic oesophagitis is diagnosed on biopsy, typically in young atopic men with food bolus impaction.
pearl: Endoscopy must always precede a diagnosis of achalasia, because a tumour at the gastro-oesophageal junction can produce an identical picture (pseudoachalasia).
thinking: Dysphagia to solids and liquids ↓ Endoscopy normal, so no structural lesion ↓ Manometry: absent peristalsis ↓ Lower oesophageal sphincter fails to relax ↓ Achalasia
exam_trap: D, Diffuse oesophageal spasm — it is another motility disorder causing dysphagia and chest pain, but the sphincter relaxes normally and contractions are present rather than absent.
takeaway: Absent peristalsis with failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation on manometry confirms achalasia.

stem:
In the outpatient clinic, a 34-year-old man who was recently diagnosed with achalasia asks what has actually gone wrong with his gullet. He has been bringing back undigested food when he lies down at night and has been sleeping propped up on pillows.

Which abnormality best explains his condition?

options.A: Frequent transient relaxations of the lower oesophageal sphincter allowing acid into the oesophagus
options.B: Fibrous narrowing of the lower oesophagus caused by repeated acid injury
options.C: Loss of inhibitory neurones in the myenteric plexus, so the lower oesophageal sphincter fails to relax and peristalsis is lost
options.D: Eosinophilic infiltration of the oesophageal wall triggered by food allergens
options.E: Overproduction of gastric acid by parietal cells

correct_answer: C. Loss of inhibitory neurones in the myenteric plexus, so the lower oesophageal sphincter fails to relax and peristalsis is lost
why_correct: Achalasia results from degeneration of inhibitory nitrergic neurones in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus. Without them the lower oesophageal sphincter cannot relax on swallowing and the oesophageal body loses its peristalsis, so food and fluid pool in a dilating oesophagus. That retained food is regurgitated when he lies flat, which is why he props himself up.
why_wrong: A. Transient sphincter relaxations are the main mechanism of gastro-oesophageal reflux, the opposite problem. B. Acid-related fibrosis produces a peptic stricture, not achalasia. D. Eosinophilic infiltration describes eosinophilic oesophagitis. E. Acid hypersecretion causes peptic ulceration, as in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, not a motility disorder.
pearl: Treatment options for achalasia include pneumatic balloon dilatation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy or peroral endoscopic myotomy, with botulinum toxin injection reserved for those unfit for these.
thinking: Known achalasia ↓ Nocturnal regurgitation of undigested food ↓ Food retained above a closed sphincter ↓ Sphincter cannot relax and peristalsis is absent ↓ Loss of inhibitory myenteric neurones
exam_trap: A, Transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations — the phrase mentions the sphincter and regurgitation, but excessive relaxation causes reflux, whereas achalasia is a failure to relax.
takeaway: Achalasia is caused by loss of myenteric inhibitory neurones, leaving a non-relaxing lower oesophageal sphincter and aperistalsis.

stem:
A GP registrar is reviewing a 59-year-old woman who has been referred for difficulty swallowing. Before reading the endoscopy report, he wants to decide from the history whether a structural narrowing of the oesophagus is more likely than a disorder of oesophageal muscle function.

Which feature of her history would most support a structural narrowing?

options.A: Difficulty with liquids as much as solids from the very first episode
options.B: Coughing and spluttering as soon as she tries to swallow
options.C: Trouble that started with solid food and has gradually come to involve liquids
options.D: Symptoms that come and go from day to day
options.E: Episodes of central chest pain triggered by very cold drinks

correct_answer: C. Trouble that started with solid food and has gradually come to involve liquids
why_correct: A fixed obstruction such as a tumour or stricture first impedes bulky solids; as the lumen narrows further, softer foods and finally liquids are affected. This progressive solids-then-liquids pattern is the classic history of mechanical obstruction and, in someone of her age, needs urgent investigation for cancer.
why_wrong: A. Liquids and solids affected equally from the start suggest a motility disorder such as achalasia. B. Coughing at the start of a swallow indicates oropharyngeal dysphagia, often neurological. D. Fluctuating symptoms are more typical of a motility disorder than a fixed lesion. E. Pain triggered by cold drinks suggests oesophageal spasm, a motility problem.
pearl: Ask three questions in dysphagia: is it oropharyngeal or oesophageal, solids first or both from the start, and intermittent or progressive.
thinking: Need to separate structural from motility causes ↓ Structural lesions narrow the lumen gradually ↓ Bulky solids are affected first ↓ Liquids follow as narrowing worsens ↓ Solids then liquids means mechanical obstruction
exam_trap: A, Liquids and solids from the start — it sounds like more severe dysphagia, but it is the hallmark of a motility disorder, not a fixed obstruction.
takeaway: Progressive dysphagia that begins with solids and later involves liquids indicates mechanical obstruction.

stem:
A 49-year-old woman with long-standing heavy periods tells her GP that solid food catches high up, just below her throat. On examination she has cracks at the corners of her mouth, a smooth sore tongue and spoon-shaped nails. Blood tests show a microcytic anaemia with a low ferritin. A barium swallow shows a thin membrane partly occluding the upper oesophagus.

Which condition best explains these findings?
why_correct: Plummer–Vinson (Paterson–Brown-Kelly) syndrome is the triad of iron-deficiency anaemia, dysphagia and a post-cricoid oesophageal web. Her angular cheilitis, glossitis and koilonychia are signs of iron deficiency, likely from menorrhagia, and the web seen on barium swallow explains the high dysphagia.
why_wrong: B. Coeliac disease can cause iron deficiency through malabsorption but does not produce oesophageal webs. C. Achalasia causes dysphagia to solids and liquids with a dilated oesophagus, not a web. D. A pharyngeal pouch causes regurgitation, halitosis and a gurgling neck swelling, and is a pouch rather than a membrane. E. Systemic sclerosis causes distal oesophageal dysmotility with reflux, usually with Raynaud's phenomenon and skin thickening.
pearl: Plummer–Vinson syndrome carries an increased risk of post-cricoid squamous cell carcinoma, so endoscopic assessment and follow-up are needed in addition to iron replacement.
thinking: Dysphagia felt high in the oesophagus ↓ Signs of iron deficiency: cheilitis, glossitis, koilonychia ↓ Microcytic anaemia with low ferritin ↓ Thin upper oesophageal web on barium swallow ↓ Plummer–Vinson syndrome
exam_trap: B, Coeliac disease — it is a classic cause of unexplained iron deficiency, but it does not cause an oesophageal web or dysphagia.
takeaway: Iron-deficiency anaemia with dysphagia from a post-cricoid web is Plummer–Vinson syndrome, a premalignant condition.

stem:
A 62-year-old man with obesity and more than twenty years of heartburn tells the practice nurse at his annual review that, in recent weeks, mouthfuls of food sometimes seem to lodge low behind his breastbone before passing. He has never had an endoscopy.

Which complication of his chronic reflux is most important to exclude urgently?
why_correct: Chronic reflux, male sex, obesity and older age are risk factors for Barrett's oesophagus and progression to oesophageal adenocarcinoma. New dysphagia in this setting may mean a malignant stricture, so cancer must be excluded first through a suspected cancer pathway referral for endoscopy. A benign peptic stricture is the main alternative.
why_wrong: B. Barrett's oesophagus without dysplasia is premalignant but is usually asymptomatic and does not itself cause dysphagia, nor does it need urgent exclusion. C. A sliding hiatus hernia worsens reflux but is not an urgent diagnosis and seldom causes dysphagia. D. Eosinophilic oesophagitis is not a complication of reflux and usually affects younger atopic patients. E. Candidiasis causes painful swallowing in immunosuppressed patients and is not a complication of reflux.
pearl: Adenocarcinoma, linked to reflux and Barrett's, typically arises in the lower third of the oesophagus, whereas squamous cell carcinoma, linked to smoking and alcohol, is more often in the upper and middle thirds.
thinking: Long-standing reflux in an older obese man ↓ New dysphagia ↓ Reflux leads to Barrett's then adenocarcinoma ↓ Malignancy is the complication that cannot be missed ↓ Exclude adenocarcinoma urgently
exam_trap: B, Barrett's oesophagus — it is the classic complication of chronic reflux, but it does not cause dysphagia and is not the condition that needs urgent exclusion.
takeaway: New dysphagia on a background of chronic reflux must be investigated urgently to exclude oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

stem:
On the second day of her admission to the surgical ward with gallstone pancreatitis, a 39-year-old woman complains of tingling around her lips and in her fingers. When the blood pressure cuff is inflated, her wrist and fingers go into spasm.

Which electrolyte disturbance, caused by fat necrosis in and around the pancreas, best explains these features?
why_correct: In acute pancreatitis, released lipases break down peripancreatic fat into free fatty acids, which bind calcium to form calcium soaps (saponification). The resulting fall in serum calcium causes perioral paraesthesia and carpal spasm on cuff inflation (Trousseau's sign). A low calcium is also one of the markers of severity in the Glasgow score.
why_wrong: A. Hypokalaemia causes muscle weakness and arrhythmias rather than tetany and is not caused by fat necrosis. C. Hypermagnesaemia causes weakness and loss of reflexes, not tetany; it is low magnesium that can accompany low calcium. D. Hypernatraemia causes thirst and confusion and is not a feature of fat necrosis. E. Hyperphosphataemia is not caused by saponification.
pearl: Check albumin-adjusted calcium and magnesium together, since hypomagnesaemia impairs parathyroid hormone release and makes hypocalcaemia hard to correct.
thinking: Acute pancreatitis ↓ Perioral tingling and carpal spasm with the cuff ↓ Tetany suggests low calcium ↓ Lipases cause fat necrosis ↓ Calcium is bound as soaps: hypocalcaemia
exam_trap: C, Hypermagnesaemia — magnesium disturbance does accompany pancreatitis, but it is low magnesium that occurs and a high level would cause weakness, not tetany.
takeaway: Fat necrosis in acute pancreatitis binds calcium and can cause symptomatic hypocalcaemia.

stem:
On the second day of an admission for gallstone pancreatitis, a 49-year-old woman complains of tingling around her lips and in her fingertips. Her serum albumin is normal, but her adjusted calcium has fallen below the reference range.

Which process best explains this change?

options.A: Raised parathyroid hormone release from the inflamed gland
options.B: Enhanced calcium uptake from the small intestine
options.C: Mineralocorticoid excess causing renal calcium loss
options.E: Saponification, in which free fatty acids from necrotic fat bind calcium

correct_answer: E. Saponification, in which free fatty acids from necrotic fat bind calcium
why_correct: Pancreatic lipases released into the peritoneum digest surrounding fat, freeing fatty acids that combine with calcium to form insoluble soaps. This sequesters calcium and lowers the serum level, producing perioral and digital paraesthesia. Because her albumin is normal, the fall is a true reduction rather than a binding artefact.
why_wrong: A. A rise in parathyroid hormone would push calcium up, not down. B. Greater intestinal absorption would raise serum calcium. C. Mineralocorticoids act on sodium and potassium handling, not calcium. D. Breaking down calcitonin would, if anything, tend to raise calcium.
pearl: Hypocalcaemia is one of the markers of severity in the Glasgow-Imrie score, so a falling calcium in pancreatitis suggests a more severe attack.
thinking: Pancreatitis with new paraesthesia ↓ Low adjusted calcium with normal albumin ↓ Lipases released into surrounding tissue ↓ Fatty acids complex with calcium as soaps ↓ Saponification explains the hypocalcaemia
exam_trap: A, Raised parathyroid hormone release — it sounds like a calcium-related hormone change, but PTH raises calcium; in pancreatitis the PTH response may even be blunted.
takeaway: Fat necrosis with calcium soap formation is the key mechanism of hypocalcaemia in acute pancreatitis.
